claims.text: Differences in deformation behavior among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its FCC quaternary and ternary subsets arise primarily from variations in short-range order and accompanying local lattice distortions.
Differences in failure behavior among the quinary alloy and its subsets arise primarily from variations in short-range order and local lattice distortions.
The number of constituent elements alone is not the primary determinant of the alloys' mechanical behavior.
The controlled comparison will use equiatomic, single-phase FCC quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys produced by identical thermomechanical processing.
Identical thermomechanical processing will provide comparable grain structures and phase purity across the alloys.
Reducing the system from five constituents to equiatomic four- and three-constituent subsets alters the local chemical environment.
Reducing the number and identity of constituents changes the propensity for short-range-order formation.
Mechanical testing will be performed at controlled temperature, constant strain rate, and common processing history.
Short-range order and local lattice distortions modulate resistance to dislocation glide.
Changes in alloy composition alter interatomic chemical affinities, which influence the degree and nature of short-range order.
Increased short-range order produces heterogeneous local lattice strains.
Short-range order and associated local lattice strains act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Greater short-range order and dislocation resistance increase yield strength.
Greater short-range order modifies strain-hardening behavior.
Relative to equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi, quaternary or ternary subsets with enhanced short-range order will have higher yield strength and greater resistance to dislocation motion.
Quaternary or ternary subsets with reduced short-range order will show lower yield strength or strain-hardening response relative to the quinary baseline.
The proposed effects apply under isothermal, constant-strain-rate conditions in a regime dominated by thermally activated dislocation glide.
At higher temperatures or different strain-rate regimes, thermal activation may overcome short-range-order barriers and minimize their mechanical effect.
Absence of measurable SRO differences, or absence of correlation between SRO/local distortion and mechanical-property differences, would falsify SRO as the primary driver.
